newsitem.title: PERU: Peru captures key rebels, biggest arms haul.
newsitem.headline: Peru captures key rebels, biggest arms haul.

text.p: Peruvian security forces captured the military leaders of two key Maoist Shining Path units during a massive operation in the guerrillas' jungle heartland, anti-terrorist police sources said on Thursday.
The sweep, which has been going on for a week, also brought the biggest guerrilla arms haul in Peru since the start of Shining Path's uprising in 1980, the sources added.
The exact number of rebels caught was not known but the operation concentrated on the leaders rather than rank and file members, the sources said.

They said the now-leaderless units were responsible for controlling the dense jungle around Mohena and Pucayacu, 200 miles (320 km) northeast of Lima, where Shining Path's top decision-making body usually operates.
"Here it is not soldiers that have been caught, it is generals," one anti-terrorist police source said.
The army also located several large arms caches, capturing over 30 anti-tank rockets, a few anti-aircraft rockets, one mortar, over 30 rifles, 300 grenades, and 9,000 bullets.
"We have taken the largest amount of arms and ammunition in the whole anti-terrorist fight," one source said. "Their armed power has suffered a tremendous blow."

The blow against Shining Path coincided with recent attacks by the group in Lima that raised fears the guerrillas were beginning a new campaign of violence. Last week, they exploded a huge car bomb at a police station in a shanty town, injuring at least eight officers, and on Tuesday shot to death one policeman patrolling a suburb.

In the jungle operation, the army used police intelligence information to locate on Friday the leaders of a unit known in Spanish as Cuchara (Spoon). Patrols waited in the Mohena jungle forest until the early hours of Saturday before pouncing on the rebels as they slept.

Without firing a bullet, the soldiers captured four of the unit leaders including its chief, known as "Teacher," who had special responsibility for the personal security of "Comrade Artemio" -- Shining Path's military leader in its Huallaga valley heartland.
The second capture involved leaders of a unit that had been operating in the neighbouring Pucayacu area, the sources said, without giving more details.
These two units operated with such freedom that they considered this area high in the jungle as a separate state, with whole villages under the control of Shining Path, the sources said.
The army was continuing its huge operation on Thursday, using helicopters and over 100 soldiers to sweep through the Huallaga valley hoping to flush out more rebels.
The police sources said there are five more military units that each count on up to 300 members who, while not permanently armed, take part in occasional operations in the Huallaga valley.
The operation also included a sweep around the southern department of Ayacucho, where Shining Path's commander-in-the- field Oscar Ramirez, alias "Feliciano," is believed to be hiding out.

The sources claimed the huge arms finds in Huallaga meant Shining Path in the short term would not be able to make its regular raids on jungle zones, where columns of up to 200 members can take control of isolated villages for days.

The massive army offensive's main goal is to weaken Shining Path, but security forces also hope to flush out the remaining armed members -- estimated at no more than 200 -- of the smaller Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA), the sources said.

The MRTA overshadowed the larger and more violent Shining Path with its takeover of the Japanese ambassador's home in Lima, where it held 72 hostages for four months until a spectacular military strike on April 22 that rescued all but one of their captives. All 14 MRTA hostage-takers died in the lightning raid.
